## Recent OpenVLA Interpretability Research

**Mechanistic Interpretability for Steering VLAs:**
Research projects feedforward activations within transformer layers onto the token embedding basis, identifying sparse semantic directions - such as speed and direction - that are causally linked to action selection. This method has been evaluated on OpenVLA, demonstrating zero-shot behavioral control in simulation (LIBERO) and on a physical robot (UR5).

**Emergent World Representations:**
Evidence suggests a linear world model in OpenVLA, motivating a practical pipeline for interpretable planning where the model's intended action is translated into an explicit prediction about how the environment representation will change.

VLAs process heterogeneous token sequences interleaving vision, language, and proprioception, and mean-pooling activations across token positions destroys action-critical information, causing catastrophic task failure despite high reconstruction quality.

**Event-Grounded Sparse Autoencoders:**
Event-grounded sparse autoencoder (SAE) analysis grounded in closed-loop behavioral events yields the strongest causal effects on OpenVLA and transfers to other models.

Representational collapse refers to the degradation of generalizable representations from pre-trained models as they are fine-tuned for a specific end task. This can lead to instability, sub-optimal performance, and weak generalization.

One approach uses trust region theory with parametric noise to discourage representation change during fine-tuning without hurting performance. Additionally, Representation Projection Invariance (REPINA) is a novel regularization method to maintain information content of representation and reduce representation collapse during fine-tuning.

**Title:** Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models

**Authors:** Bryce Grant, Xijia Zhao, and Peng Wang from Case Western Reserve University

**Submission Date:** March 19, 2026

**Overview:** The paper studies how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine perception, language, and motor control in a single architecture to translate multimodal inputs into actions.

**Methodology:** The researchers apply activation injection, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and linear probes to six models spanning 80M-7B parameters across 394,000+ rollout episodes on four benchmarks.

**Key Findings:**
- The visual pathway dominates action generation across all architectures, with injecting baseline activations into null-prompt episodes recovering near-identical behavior
- Language sensitivity depends on task structure, not model design—when visual context uniquely specifies the task, language is ignored; when multiple goals share a scene, language becomes essential
- In multi-pathway architectures, expert pathways encode motor programs while VLM pathways encode goal semantics

The paper also includes a resource called Action Atlas for interactive exploration of these findings.

Fine-tuning vision-language models (VLMs) on robot teleoperation data to create vision-language-action (VLA) models suffers from a fundamental tradeoff: learning to produce actions often diminishes the VLM's foundational reasoning and multimodal understanding, hindering generalization to novel scenarios, instruction following, and semantic understanding.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Vision-language-action models.}
VLAs fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual and language input~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024,black2024_pi0,zheng2024tracevla,hung2025nora,xiao2025ava}.
NLP instruction tuning is well-characterized behaviorally~\cite{wei2022finetuned,ouyang2022training}, but the representational effects of VLA fine-tuning remain unexamined.
Fine-tuning operates in a low intrinsic dimension~\cite{aghajanyan2021intrinsic} and can distort pretrained features~\cite{kumar2022finetuning}; recent VLA-specific work proposes representation-preserving strategies~\cite{grover2025preserving}. Existing analyses target single architectures and cannot separate training dynamics from backbone artifacts.

\paragraph{Mechanistic and behavioral analysis.}
Mechanistic interpretability has revealed residual stream communication~\cite{elhage2021}, induction heads~\cite{olsson2022}, and task circuits~\cite{wang2023_ioi,conmy2023}; causal tracing localizes factual recall~\cite{meng2022_rome}; attention probing shows heads encode syntactic relations~\cite{clark2019} and most can be pruned~\cite{michel2019sixteen}.
In VLMs, recent work characterizes visual token redundancy~\cite{fan2026visual} and progressive visual-textual alignment~\cite{neo2025interpreting,long2026understanding}.
Behavioral evaluations of VLAs reveal visual dominance~\cite{grant2026,hou2026,fei2025}; mechanistic studies identify sparse semantic directions~\cite{haon2025}, interpretable features~\cite{swann2026,buurmeijer2026}, symbolic representations~\cite{lu2025,molinari2025}, and comprehension-action trade-offs~\cite{fang2025}.
Concurrent continual-learning studies find that pretrained VLAs resist forgetting under sequential fine-tuning~\cite{liu2026forgetting}, consistent with our observation that VLA-to-VLA transitions preserve exit-layer structure.
All prior representational analyses target a single architecture; our $3 \times 4$ cross-architecture matrix tests whether mechanisms replicate across backbone families.

\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
Two concurrent studies address complementary aspects of VLA understanding.
Fang et al.~\cite{fang2026when} construct a behavioral benchmark of counterfactual instruction failures on LIBERO and propose inference-time mitigation; their evaluation measures \emph{whether} the model follows the correct instruction, while our counterfactual perturbation measures \emph{how much} hidden-state geometry changes under instruction replacement (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}), providing a representational sensitivity metric rather than a behavioral success metric.
Our analysis thus provides the internal representational basis that may underlie the vision-override patterns they observe.
Buurmeijer et al.~\cite{buurmeijer2026} probe low-level motor features (position, gripper state) in OpenVLA via linear probes and explicitly identify abstract semantic features as future work; instruction-level routing is the focus of our analysis.
We additionally distinguish training-associated from inherited effects through trained/reference contrasts across three architectures, a decomposition absent from prior single-architecture studies.

\paragraph{Probing and similarity methodology.}
RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, CKA~\cite{kornblith2019}, and linear probes~\cite{alain2017,belinkov2022} provide complementary geometric and functional evaluation.
We adopt RSA and MLP probes (CKA in appendix); the two metrics can diverge on the same data (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_appendix}), and Cohen's $d$ vs.\ cosine distance are not comparable across trained/reference conditions (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
